citation: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2023). Good Behavior Game. https://whatworks.ed.gov
title: Team-based interdependent group contingency game structure
description: The Good Behavior Game follows a recurring session structure: "Teachers divided their students into teams and reviewed the expected behaviors and rules of the game. Teachers monitored student behavior during the game and scored the teams based on how well they followed the rules. At the end of the session, winning teams received a reward." Rules typically include staying seated and on task, following directions, being polite, and ignoring distractions, displayed on a poster. Teachers choose scoring methods (adding or subtracting points), constant or variable winning goals, and reward timing. Variations in the reviewed studies included a whole-class-as-one-team version and placing individual students on their own team.
requirements: Teachers describe and remind students of game rules and winning criteria before starting the game, as done in all 16 reviewed studies
Teachers provide rewards to winning teams, as done in all 16 reviewed studies
constraints: In the reviewed studies the game was played during the school day in 15 studies and in an after-school program in one study
target_learners: Students in grades K-11 classrooms, including whole classes and focal students with high levels of disruptive behavior
target_learning_goals: Reducing disruptive behavior and rule violations
examples: In six studies teachers offered winning students small prizes such as snacks, school supplies, stickers, or lip balm; in three studies teachers offered classroom privileges such as free time
key_sources: What Works Clearinghouse, Institute of Education Sciences, U.S. Department of Education. (2023). Good Behavior Game. https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/InterventionReport/728

article_title: Game-based assessment: an integrated model for capturing evidence of learning in play
citation: Richard Halverson, Elizabeth Owen, Nathan Wills, R. Benjamin Shapiro. (2012). Game-Based Assessment: An integrated model for capturing evidence of learning in play. ERIA Working Paper. http://www.eriainteractive.com/index.php
title: Game-Based Assessment (GBA) model: a four-layer design strategy embedding assessment in game design
description: The GBA model is a design strategy developed by the Games, Learning and Society group to capture evidence of player learning during game play rather than treating the game as a black box. It integrates four layers: "the content-model; the game flow design; and the GBA components of the semantic template and learning telemetry." The content model outlines learning goals, game-flow design builds interaction opportunities around them, the semantic template selects which click-stream data may indicate learning, and the learning telemetry layer collects and organizes that data into player profiles for analysis against pre-post measures. It draws on evidence-centered design, stealth assessment, and education data mining.
requirements: Requires designing the game around specific learning goals and a content model agreed with content experts
Requires a semantic template built in coordination with the game-flow design specifying key moments hypothesized to yield learning evidence
Requires a telemetry layer tagging player moves so the data stream can be mapped onto the semantic template
constraints: The authors state they are not yet in a position to deliver results confirming the viability or quality of the GBA model across game spaces
The semantic template's bet-hedging role may narrow the data too severely and leave out information necessary to understanding player interaction and learning
The presentation deliberately focuses on little-g game outcomes and omits Big G social and narrative contexts of game-based learning
target_learners: middle and high school students playing learning games
general lay audiences for public science understanding
target_learning_goals: domain content learning (e.g., stem-cell science processes) embedded in game play
examples: GBA was built into Progenitor X: designers identified 15 key moments in game play and tagged each player move with button, time-stamp, flashing status, tool name, and tag type
key_sources: Richard Halverson, Elizabeth Owen, Nathan Wills, R. Benjamin Shapiro. (2012). Game-Based Assessment: An integrated model for capturing evidence of learning in play. ERIA Working Paper. http://www.eriainteractive.com/index.php

article_title: Using Bayesian networks to improve knowledge assessment
citation: Millán-Valldeperas, E.; Descalço, L.; Castillo, G.; Oliveira, P.; Diogo, S. (2013). Using Bayesian networks to improve knowledge assessment. Elsevier. http://hdl.handle.net/10630/7068
title: Generic Bayesian student model (GBSM) integrated into the PMatE computerized testing system
description: The GBSM is an existing generic Bayesian student model that was integrated into an existing computerized testing system within the Mathematics Education Project (PmatE) of the University of Aveiro. In this work it "had been used" to define Bayesian Student Models (BSMs) "for a concrete domain: first degree equations", with separate BSMs built for the computer test and the written exam. Its diagnosis capabilities were then evaluated against expert grading.
requirements: Requires definition of a domain-specific Bayesian student model from the generic model for the target domain
constraints: The article reports low agreement between the computer-test BSM diagnosis and the expert average
target_learners: students learning first degree equations in the PMatE system
target_learning_goals: diagnosing student knowledge of 12 concepts related to first degree equations
examples: Two BSMs were developed, one for the computer test and another for the written exam, and used to estimate students' knowledge on the same 12 concepts
key_sources: Millán-Valldeperas, E.; Descalço, L.; Castillo, G.; Oliveira, P.; Diogo, S. (2013). Using Bayesian networks to improve knowledge assessment. Elsevier. http://hdl.handle.net/10630/7068

article_title: Efficacy of Computer Games on Language Learning
citation: Blanka KLIMOVA, Jaroslav KACETL. (2017). Efficacy of Computer Games on Language Learning. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 16(4). https://www.tojet.net/
title: Distinction between game-based learning and gamification
description: The review distinguishes two concepts using Findley (2016) and Pappas (2015): game-based learning "uses game elements to teach a specific skill or achieve a specific learning outcome", fully integrating game mechanics with training content so the game is the training, whereas gamification applies game mechanics in a non-game context as a reward for completing existing training modules, to motivate and engage learners. The review uses this distinction to frame its analysis of computer games in language learning.
requirements: Game-based learning requires integration of game mechanics with the training content itself
constraints: The distinction is drawn from secondary sources (Findley, 2016; Pappas, 2015) cited by the review
key_sources: Blanka KLIMOVA, Jaroslav KACETL. (2017). Efficacy of Computer Games on Language Learning. TOJET: The Turkish Online Journal of Educational Technology, 16(4). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1160637

article_title: Measurement of Child Behavior via Classroom Observations in the Good Behavior Game Professional Development Models Randomized Control Trial
citation: Kurki, A., Wang, W., Li, Y., & Poduska, J. (2013). Measurement of Child Behavior via Classroom Observations in the Good Behavior Game Professional Development Models Randomized Control Trial. SREE Fall 2013 Conference. https://www.sree.org
title: Good Behavior Game professional development models randomized control trial (GBG Basic vs. GBG with Coach)
description: A four-year IES Goal 3 project comparing two professional development models for the Good Behavior Game, a group-based classroom behavior management strategy built around "four core elements integrating (1) classroom rules, (2) team membership, (3) monitoring of behavior, and (4) positive reinforcement to individuals and the group". GBG Basic provides 2 days of initial training plus a booster day; GBG with Coach adds 90 minutes of coaching every two weeks for one school year. Students are randomly assigned to classrooms and classrooms to GBG Basic, GBG with Coach, or control, in the multilingual Houston Independent School District.
requirements: Random assignment of students to classrooms and classrooms to conditions within virtual schools grouped by language of instruction
constraints: An unbalanced design was adopted due to the large number of bilingual classrooms; bilingual classrooms in the GBG with Coach condition received a bilingual coach and materials in English and Spanish
target_learners: first- and second-grade students in high-need elementary schools
target_learning_goals: reducing aggressive/disruptive behavior and increasing on-task behavior
examples: Cohort 1 comprised 18 schools, 71 classrooms and 1401 students, including 36 bilingual and 35 regular education classrooms
key_sources: Kurki, A., Wang, W., Li, Y., & Poduska, J. (2013). Measurement of Child Behavior via Classroom Observations in the Good Behavior Game Professional Development Models Randomized Control Trial. SREE Fall 2013 Conference. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED563300

article_title: Game-Based Assessment of Cognitive Abilities and Personality Characteristics for Surgical Resident Selection: A Preliminary Validation Study.
citation: Gazit N, Ben-Gal G, Eliashar R. (2025). Game-Based Assessment of Cognitive Abilities and Personality Characteristics for Surgical Resident Selection: A Preliminary Validation Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/72264
title: Game-based assessment test (Dotto, CurioCity, MultiTask) measuring 14 surgical-resident competencies
description: A gamified test built with Benchmark.games consisting of three video games — Dotto, CurioCity, and MultiTask — adapted to assess 14 competencies such as planning, problem-solving, analytical thinking, flexibility, multitasking, working memory, and precision. Each game elicits behaviors relevant to two or more competencies, with "precision, which was assessed in all 3 games". Approximately 2000 data points are recorded per 15-minute gameplay session, transformed into higher-level variables and aggregated into competency scores standardized on a norm of over 5000 observations, presented on a scale of 1-10.
requirements: Administration on a standard computer with a stable internet connection and a mouse
Written instructions and video demonstrations in English, with a few minutes of practice before each game
A norm database for standardizing competency scores
constraints: Does not assess competencies not susceptible to computerized measurement, such as interpersonal skills, teamwork, leadership, and integrity
Tasks were primarily procedural and did not involve verbal abilities
Test takes about 45-60 minutes to complete
target_learners: Medical interns applying for surgical residency
target_learning_goals: Assessment of cognitive abilities and personality characteristics relevant to surgical resident selection
examples: In the study, 152 medical interns completed the test alongside a Lap-X VR laparoscopic technical aptitude test, and 30 expert surgeons reviewed the test and completed feedback questionnaires
key_sources: Gazit N, Ben-Gal G, Eliashar R. (2025). Game-Based Assessment of Cognitive Abilities and Personality Characteristics for Surgical Resident Selection: A Preliminary Validation Study. JMIR Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.2196/72264
